main_point: Police raids and legal pressure in Europe are forcing filesharing link sites to close, proving that hosting such sites is illegal even if the files themselves are not stored on the servers.

aliases: trade association representing the interests of major movie studios based in the United States

statements.text: European law enforcement agencies, acting on pressure from copyright organizations, have conducted raids and issued legal threats that are compelling filesharing link sites in countries like the Netherlands, Finland, and Slovenia to shut down. These actions demonstrate that hosting such sites is considered illegal, even though the servers do not store the actual copyrighted files, thereby closing a potential legal loophole for users.
statements.text_short: European police raids and legal pressure are forcing filesharing link sites to close, proving that hosting them is illegal.

statements.text: The operators of the Slovenian-based BitTorrent site SuprNova.org decided to voluntarily shut down their link distribution service following reports of arrests against other site administrators and after receiving formal legal warnings from copyright enforcement groups. This decision was made to avoid the risk of having their servers seized by authorities, even though the site's owners maintain that hosting links to unauthorized files is not inherently illegal under Slovenian law.
statements.text_short: Copyright enforcement groups issued formal legal warnings. Other site administrators faced arrest reports. In response, the operators of SuprNova.org, a BitTorrent site based in Slovenia, chose to stop their link distribution service voluntarily.

statements.text: In an effort to circumvent the legal and operational risks associated with centralized hosting, the decentralized filesharing project eXeem, developed by the creators of the now-closed SuprNova.org, reached its beta stage in late 2004. This system was designed to allow users to publish and distribute files directly without relying on central servers or trackers, aiming to eliminate the specific legal vulnerability that led to the closure of the original link site.
statements.text_short: The decentralized filesharing project eXeem, developed by the creators of the now-closed SuprNova.org, reached its beta stage in late 2004 to allow users to publish and distribute files directly without relying on central servers or trackers.

statements.text: The filesharing link site TorrentBits.org was shut down around the same time as other major European sites, yet the specific reasons for its closure remain unknown. While other sites in the region were forced offline by police raids or voluntarily closed due to legal pressure, the circumstances surrounding the disappearance of TorrentBits.org have not been clarified by its founder.
statements.text_short: The filesharing link site TorrentBits.org was shut down around the same time as other major European sites, yet the specific reasons for its closure remain unknown.

statements.text: Delirium Vault, a peer-to-peer link site, has reportedly ceased operations alongside other similar services like Youceff Torrents and Phoenix Torrents, joining a wave of closures affecting sites in France, the Netherlands, Finland, and Slovenia. This pattern of shutdowns suggests that law enforcement actions are effectively dismantling these networks, even when the sites themselves do not store illegal files directly.
statements.text_short: Delirium Vault joins other closed link sites, indicating a broader trend of enforcement actions dismantling filesharing networks.

statements.text: Law enforcement agencies across Europe are utilizing police raids and legal pressure to force the closure of filesharing link sites, a strategy that demonstrates hosting such sites is illegal even if the servers do not contain the actual infringing files. This approach relies on the fact that many operators are volunteers running non-profit services who lack the resources to withstand prolonged legal battles or the loss of donated server equipment.
statements.text_short: European police raids and legal pressure are proving that hosting filesharing sites is illegal, forcing their closure even when files aren't stored on the servers.

actor_aliases: trade association representing the interests of major movie studios based in the United States
statements.text: The Motion Picture Association of America may be connected to police operations that shut down filesharing sites in Europe, though this link is not yet confirmed. While the Finnish National Bureau of Investigation says it has no contact with the trade group, the group claims responsibility for closing the Finnish site FinReactor. This creates doubt about who really drives these coordinated enforcement actions.
statements.text_short: The MPAA is suspected of linking to police actions, though official denials exist, raising questions about the true drivers behind European site closures.

actor_aliases: trade association representing the interests of major movie studios based in the United States
statements.text: FinReactor, a significant Finnish filesharing platform, was closed. The Motion Picture Association of America claims responsibility for this shutdown. However, the Finnish National Bureau of Investigation states there were no contacts between the association and Finnish authorities. This difference shows that international cooperation between copyright enforcement groups and local police forces is complicated and often disputed when shutting down digital services.
statements.text_short: The MPAA claims credit for FinReactor's closure, despite official denials from Finnish authorities regarding any contact.

statements.text: The BitTorrent system, created by programmer Bram Cohen and introduced in 2002, functions as a peer-to-peer file distribution tool that allows users to download files at high speeds by swapping file portions with one another rather than relying on a single centralised server, a design that makes it particularly effective for quickly spreading new releases to large numbers of users.
statements.text_short: BitTorrent is a 2002 peer-to-peer tool that enables fast file distribution by swapping data chunks between users instead of using a central server.

statements.text: MetaMachine created the eDonkey2000 software, which uses the Multisource File Transfer Protocol. This peer-to-peer file sharing system promotes permanent file sharing to keep files available over time. However, it is usually not as good as the BitTorrent system for quickly spreading new releases to many users.
statements.text_short: The eDonkey2000 application, developed by MetaMachine, functions as a peer-to-peer sharing tool. It values keeping files available for extended periods more than quickly spreading out fresh releases.
